title: Olen, olet, on
titleEn: I am, you are, he or she is
body: The end of the verb says who: olen is “I am”, olet is “you are”.
So minä and sinä can be left out: Olen Sofia means “I am Sofia”.

title: Olemme, olette, ovat
body: Three more endings for three more people.
te is also the polite “you” for one person.

title: En ymmärrä
titleEn: Not: a verb of its own
body: Finnish says “not” with a verb that takes the person ending: en, et, ei.
The main verb then loses its ending: puhun → en puhu.

title: Oletko?
body: Add -ko or -kö to the verb and put it first. That turns a sentence into a yes/no question.
Back-team words take -ko, front-team words take -kö, as in unit 0.

title: Espanjasta
body: “From” is an ending: -sta or -stä, matching the word’s vowel team.
Some words change a little before it: Suomi → Suomesta.

title: Turussa, Helsingissä
body: “In” is the ending -ssa or -ssä.
Some words change their middle consonant before it: Turku → Turussa, Helsinki → Helsingissä. This is called consonant gradation. For now, learn these as they come.

title: Puhun suomea
body: After puhua (to speak), the language takes -a or -ä: suomi → suomea.
This form is called the partitive. It has more uses, and they arrive one at a time: next with numbers, then with food.

title: Kaksi kahvia
body: After yksi (one), the noun stays as it is: yksi kahvi.
From kaksi (two) up, the noun takes the partitive, and stays singular: kaksi kahvia, viisi euroa.

title: Leipää ja juustoa
body: Food and drink you can’t count take the partitive: Syön leipää. Juon kahvia.
After a “not”, the thing is always partitive: En syö lihaa.

title: Kortilla
body: -lla or -llä means “on” or “at”, and also “by means of”: kortilla is “by card”.
Notice kortti → kortilla: the tt becomes one t, like rk in Turku → Turussa.

examples.en: at me, as in minulla on: I have

title: Kassin, omenan
body: When you want, take or need one whole thing, it often ends in -n: Haluan omenan. Tarvitsetko kassin?
With “some”, or after “not”, it is the partitive instead: Haluan kahvia. En tarvitse kassia.

title: Kirjaston vieressä
body: -n also means “of” or “’s”: Suomen is “of Finland, Finland’s”.
Words like vieressä (next to) need it: kirjaston vieressä, next to the library.
Same word, different jobs: Turku, Turussa, Turun.

title: Kauppaan, kotiin
titleEn: Into, to: repeat the vowel, add -n
body: Going into or to a place: repeat the last vowel and add -n. kauppa → kauppaan.
This ending keeps the strong consonant: kaupassa (in the shop) but kauppaan (into the shop).
A few words take -hin instead: töihin, to work.

title: Minulla on
body: Finnish has no verb “have”. It says “at me is”: minulla on.
The question: Onko sinulla lippu? Do you have a ticket?
